- Chairman Michael Saylor’s firm currently holds 845,050 Bitcoin, valued at approximately $65 billion.
- Leadership defended the sales as a strategic move to fund preferred stock dividends for STRC shareholders.
- The company has adopted a "two-way strategy" that allows for future Bitcoin sales to maintain balance sheet health.

### Why it Matters
This shift in strategy highlights the tension between aggressive cryptocurrency accumulation and the practical financial requirements of managing corporate debt and shareholder dividends. By prioritizing liquidity over pure market timing, MicroStrategy is attempting to balance its role as a major Bitcoin holder with its obligations as a publicly traded company.

articles.title: Trump Administration Sides With OpenAI in Publishers’ Copyright Lawsuits
articles.author: Jon Reed
articles.content:
The Trump administration has weighed in on a series of copyright disputes between news organizations and OpenAI, supporting the ChatGPT-maker’s position that its use of publishers’ content to train AI models constituted fair use.
The statement of interest of the United States (PDF) was filed Tuesday in a series of cases in the US District Court for the Southern District of New York, including one initiated by The New York Times and another by Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company. Ziff Davis filed the suit in 2025, alleging OpenAI infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.
In its filing, the federal government said a ruling in publishers’ favor could hinder AI development, limit competition among AI firms and hurt the country’s competitiveness with foreign developers.
“Rules of law that make it significantly more difficult to develop a robust AI industry in the United States … threaten national security and give a competitive advantage to foreign adversaries who are not so encumbered,” the filing states.
Graham James, a spokesperson for The New York Times, told CNET in a statement that the administration is “siding with a handful of trillion-dollar AI companies” instead of American creators and that doing so undermines both creators and AI developers.
“Both AI and creators can thrive – AI companies simply need to pay fairly for the content that makes their products possible, as copyright law requires,” James said. “The Administration’s proposal to let companies take that content without permission or compensation would undermine the sustainability of the human-created content that a healthy society depends on, and which AI needs to function.”
CNET has reached out to representatives for OpenAI and Ziff Davis for comment.
The Times initiated the lawsuit at the end of 2023, a year after ChatGPT’s debut. In its initial complaint (PDF), the news organization said large language models, such as those that power ChatGPT, were built using content that included millions of its articles. That training constituted an effort to “free-ride” on the Times’ investment in journalism and create products that compete.
The government said it sees LLMs’ ability to help others compete with large media corporations as a positive development. It cited independent authors using AI models to generate images that might otherwise require a photographer or license, and LLMs directing users to “dissenting sources that offer contrary information or perspectives.”
“It is not in the public’s interest for the largest technology companies to have an oligopoly on LLM training due to licensing entry barriers that function primarily as large subsidies for old mainstream media companies,” the government stated.
Major media companies aren’t the only ones who’ve sued OpenAI over copyright infringement. Authors, including big names like George R.R. Martin, have also accused the company of using their works in model training. OpenAI rival Anthropic, which makes Claude, settled piracy claims with authors for $1.5 billion, although a judge ruled the company’s use of copyrighted material was fair use.
Earlier this summer, publishers accused OpenAI of withholding evidence about how it trains its models, claims the company has denied.
articles.summary:
The Trump administration filed a statement of interest in federal court supporting OpenAI’s argument that using copyrighted news content to train artificial intelligence models constitutes fair use.

### Key Points
- The U.S. government filed its statement in the Southern District of New York regarding lawsuits from The New York Times and Ziff Davis.
- Federal officials argue that requiring licenses for training data could hinder domestic AI development and provide a competitive advantage to foreign adversaries.
- The filing suggests that AI models promote competition by allowing smaller entities to challenge the dominance of established media corporations.
- The New York Times criticized the administration's stance, arguing that AI companies should compensate creators for the content used to build their products.
- OpenAI faces ongoing legal challenges from various publishers and authors, including George R.R. Martin, over the unauthorized use of copyrighted works.

### Why it Matters
This legal intervention highlights a growing tension between the protection of intellectual property and the rapid expansion of the domestic artificial intelligence industry. A judicial ruling in favor of fair use could significantly lower barriers to entry for AI developers while potentially reducing revenue streams for traditional media organizations.

articles.title: Tim Cook scores $47 million pay deal to stay on as Apple's chairman
articles.author: Theron Mohamed
articles.content:
Tim Cook is no longer Apple's CEO, but he'll continue to collect a CEO-sized paycheck.
This week, Cook handed Apple's reins to John Ternus after 15 years in charge, and took on the role of executive chair.
Cook's new job pays a $2 million salary instead of $3 million, and comes with an annual equity award with a target value of $45 million for fiscal 2027, Apple said in a regulatory filing on Tuesday.
Half of that award comprises performance-based restricted stock units (RSUs) that will vest based on Apple's total shareholder return relative to other S&P 500 companies. The other half is time-based and will vest over a four-year period.
As CEO, Cook earned around $74 million — including $14 million in cash bonuses and other compensation — in each of 2024 and 2025
Apple disclosed that Ternus will receive a $3 million annual salary and restricted stock with a target value of $55 million for his first year as CEO. A full 75% of the RSUs will be tied to Apple's relative performance, while 25% will vest over four years.
The iPhone maker didn't say how much Ternus and Cook stand to earn in cash bonuses.
The Buffett approach
The size of Cook's pay package signals he'll continue to play a central role at Apple.
Warren Buffett has taken a similar approach at Berkshire Hathaway, retiring as CEO at the turn of this year but staying on as chairman, serving as a close advisor to new CEO Greg Abel, and even picking stocks for Berkshire's portfolio.
Cook's compensation as chairman can also be seen as a reflection of the value he created for Apple. As CEO, he scaled Apple's manufacturing and distribution, strengthened its global supply chain, and successfully catered to China's burgeoning middle class.
Apple's split-adjusted stock price rocketed by nearly 2,300% during his tenure, from about $13 to $317 at the close of Cook's last day as CEO on Monday. It closed almost 3% higher at $325 on Tuesday.
That performance has fueled huge gains for shareholders. Buffett said during Berkshire's shareholder meeting in May that, under Cook, his $35 billion investment in Apple grew to $185 billion in value before taxes, including dividends.
"Tim Cook has made Berkshire a lot more than I have made Berkshire," Buffett told his shareholders last year.
Cook has also cultivated strong relationships with President Donald Trump and the Chinese government, which helped Apple navigate geopolitical turmoil in recent years. Ternus might call on him to work those connections in the future.
As Ternus grapples with challenges such as nailing down Apple's AI strategy and halting its talent exodus, Apple's senior leadership may have decided that keeping Cook on the payroll is worth the price.
articles.summary:
Tim Cook has transitioned from his role as Apple CEO to executive chair, passing leadership to John Ternus while maintaining a significant compensation package and advisory position.

### Key Points
- John Ternus has officially succeeded Tim Cook as Apple CEO after Cook’s 15-year tenure.
- Cook will receive a $2 million annual salary and a $45 million target equity award in his new role as executive chair.
- Incoming CEO John Ternus will earn a $3 million salary with a $55 million target equity award for his first year.
- Apple’s stock price increased by approximately 2,300% during Cook’s leadership, rising from $13 to $317 per share.
- Cook’s compensation package includes performance-based restricted stock units tied to Apple’s total shareholder return relative to the S&P 500.

### Why it Matters
Retaining Cook as executive chair ensures continuity for Apple as the company navigates complex geopolitical relationships and develops its long-term artificial intelligence strategy. This transition mirrors the succession model used by Warren Buffett at Berkshire Hathaway, signaling that Cook will remain a vital strategic advisor to the new leadership.

articles.title: More than 153 million drivers licenses on sale after "breach" at identity verification service
articles.author: Rob Beschizza
articles.content:
An identity verification company is understood to have lost more than 153 million scans of U.S. and Canadian drivers' licenses, which are now available to buy on the dark web. KrebsOnSecurity reports that the FBI is investigating the source of the images, advertised by a new user on the Russian cybercrime forum Exploit. Also in the haul are more than 10 million ID cards, more than 3 million travel documents/foreign IDs, and at least 579,000 medical cards.
A quick look around Nexus finds they are likely not exaggerating about that 153 million number: Running a blank search in Nexus (with no search parameters entered) returns approximately 11.5 million pages of results, with roughly 15 results displayed per page. It includes documents from people in both Canada and the United States, but the bulk of these records are on Americans: searching for just Canadian drivers licenses returns approximately 1.1 million results, with the largest concentration from Ontario (473,673 records).
The name of the identity verification provider isn't disclosed by the seller, and it has not announced itself. KrebsOnSecurity's own informal investigation found that idscan.net provides relevant services to retailers and services implicated by those exposed in the dataset, with scans made by Hertz car rentals and dispensary chain Planet13 (which uses idscan excusively) among the clearest signals.
What better time to be reminded that "age verification" and "identity verification" are functionally the same thing, and if the companies doing it for major retailers and airport rentals are this soaked, the ones providing cheap compliance services for everyday websites won't be dry.
Previously:
• Facebook leak exposes personal info on 533m users
• United website breach let fliers see each others' private data
• Target ups number of customers affected by data breach to 110 million
• Elizabeth Warren proposes holding execs criminally liable for scams and data breaches
articles.summary:
An unidentified identity verification provider has suffered a massive data breach, exposing over 153 million driver’s license scans and millions of other sensitive documents on the dark web.

### Key Points
- The stolen dataset includes 153 million U.S. and Canadian driver's license scans, 10 million ID cards, and 579,000 medical cards.
- Data is currently being advertised for sale by an anonymous user on the Russian-language cybercrime forum Exploit.
- The FBI has launched an investigation into the source of the leaked images and the scope of the security failure.
- Evidence suggests the provider may be idscan.net, as the leaked files contain records from clients like Hertz and the dispensary chain Planet13.
- Preliminary analysis confirms the scale of the breach, with millions of records already verified through the seller's search interface.

### Why it Matters
This breach highlights significant vulnerabilities in the third-party identity verification services used by major retailers and rental agencies to handle sensitive consumer data. The incident underscores the growing risks associated with centralized compliance services and the potential for widespread identity theft when these providers fail to secure their databases.

articles.title: Data center backlash is panicking tech oligarchs ahead of midterms
articles.author: Amanda Marcotte
articles.content:
Midterm elections are typically sleepier than presidential campaign years, so it’s genuinely shocking to see how much money is being unleashed, especially into GOP coffers, by the hyper-wealthy this cycle. Corporate political donations have reached a record of $646 million this cycle, which is 40% above what was spent on the 2024 presidential election from this sector. Another $1 billion — and likely much more — has been spent by dark money donors. While some of this money goes to Democrats, Republicans are by far the bigger beneficiaries, as moneyed interests focus their immense resources on trying to stop what looks very much to be a blue wave election.
The amount of money being thrown around by tech oligarchs is staggering — however, it’s important to remember that this is a sign of weakness.
At first blush, this torrent of spending is a little odd. Donald Trump will still be president for the next two years, making it impossible even for a robust Democratic majority in Congress to raise taxes on the rich, the concern that usually drives such campaign meddling. What’s going on become much clearer looking over the industries driving the spending, at least what can be traced publicly: over half of the corporate spending comes from the tech industry, specifically companies that invest in AI, cryptocurrency and online gambling. The pattern suggests that Silicon Valley is focused on destroying the burgeoning movement for tech accountability, before it has a chance to grow enough in power to actually pass laws constraining the industry once a Democrat retakes the White House.
Blame data centers. These giant computer campuses, which are mostly void of human beings, have become a focal point of the growing revolt against an increasingly predatory tech industry. Voters from across the political spectrum hate data centers, which consume land, water and electricity while giving little to nothing back to the community. It’s a perfect symbol of Silicon Valley’s turn to vampiric capitalism, which is no longer about building a better future, but instead maximizing how quickly they can suck the public dry of its wealth and resources. The more voters learn about data centers, the more they oppose them. In March, a Gallup poll even found that 71% of Americans oppose data centers in their community, more than they oppose a local nuclear power plant.
Want more Amanda Marcotte on politics? Sign up for her free newsletter, Standing Room Only, now also on YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.
Because data centers are a local and state issue, citizens are finding they have real leverage in protesting their construction. Both Democratic and Republican politicians who had previously been supportive of data centers are now scrambling to oppose them, or at least create the appearance of opposition. Democrats have been swifter to respond to public outrage, leading Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul to put up strict roadblocks to construction. But even Republican Gov. Greg Abbott of Texas is trying to slow things down a bit.
Of course, once voters realize they have power to stop data centers, they’re more likely to realize they can also petition their government to do more — like restrict other predatory online industries such as crypto and so-called “prediction market” apps. In response, tech executives are clearly realizing that city councils and state legislatures can do a lot to constrain them. One reason the campaign spending this cycle is so out of control is that rich donors are spreading the money around, trying to buy influence over races they would have ignored in the past.
The amount of money being thrown around by tech oligarchs is staggering — however, it’s important to remember that this is a sign of weakness. They’re spending ungodly amounts of money because they’re that afraid of the power of everyday people who oppose them. Their panic is a sign that, no matter how hard Trump and his financial backers have tried to destroy democracy, it’s still alive enough to create a real threat to Silicon Valley’s power, as evidenced by the initial gains of anti-data center activists.
Tesla CEO Elon Musk is reportedly spending $200 million to boost Republicans, especially in Texas, where the data center construction has become a huge political battleground. Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz, the billionaire founders of the tech investment firm Andreessen Horowitz, have already donated over $115 million, mostly to Republicans, including $12 million to Trump’s super PAC MAGA Inc. Jeff Yass, a billionaire who has heavily invested in AI, has spent almost $94 million, mostly on Republicans, with an eye towards protecting data centers. Greg and Anna Brockman, founders of OpenAI, have donated $50 million, including $25 million to MAGA Inc.
This is just the spending that is publicly traceable. Tech investors are likely a major force driving dark money spending this election cycle as well.
Focusing the money on Republicans makes sense. While some Democrats have been open to playing all with anti-regulation tech donors, they are facing growing resistance from inside the party that is turning those donations into a poison pill, more likely to hurt than harm a candidate. Republicans have always been an anti-regulation party devoted to serving the rich at the expense of everyone else, making them a natural fit for Silicon Valley donors.
The lavish spending is certainly paying off in the GOP ranks. Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Tex., recently denounced the anti-data center movement as driven by “hardcore left-wing values.” On Monday, Vice President JD Vance dismissed the opposition to data centers as an easily resolved dispute over power usage, and insisted “they’re an important part of the AI economy.” (That’s why people hate them, JD!) Trump, with his usual contempt for voters, sneered that opponents of data centers will be “backwards and poor,” saying that those who want to be “successful and rich” will “let Data Reign.”
Trump is heavily invested in crypto schemes that have enriched him while other investors lost money, and likely knows it’s false that this latest round of scammy tech products will enrich anyone but an elite few. He’s just employing the classic false promises of any grifter running a get-rich-quick scheme. But this time, it seems like even some Trump voters aren’t buying it. At least, that’s how other Republican politicians seem to feel. Most of them are scrambling to get on the right side of this issue, and, publicly at least, are speaking negatively about data centers.
Thus, the tech industry’s spending. The tech elite are likely hoping that they can convince Republican politicians to betray their own voters and focus their favors on the donor class once in office. But the size of the spending betrays how worried they are about people power. They clearly think it will take a lot of money to drown out the increasingly loud voices of everyday voters who see clearly that the tech industry is predatory, and are demanding that government do something about it. This midterm will be a test of who can be louder: people or money. So far, the people have the momentum.

about tech
articles.summary:
Corporate political donations have reached a record $646 million this cycle, with tech industry leaders heavily funding Republican candidates to protect AI, cryptocurrency, and data center interests.

### Key Points
- Corporate political spending has surged 40% compared to the 2024 presidential election, with over half of traceable funds originating from the tech sector.
- Major donors include Elon Musk ($200 million), Andreessen Horowitz founders ($115 million), Jeff Yass ($94 million), and OpenAI founders Greg and Anna Brockman ($50 million).
- Public opposition to data centers is high, with a Gallup poll showing 71% of Americans oppose their construction in local communities.
- Tech executives are targeting state and local races to preemptively block regulations on AI, cryptocurrency, and online gambling industries.
- While Republican leadership, including Donald Trump and JD Vance, has defended data centers, some GOP officials are distancing themselves due to voter backlash.

### Why it Matters
This record-breaking influx of capital highlights a strategic effort by tech oligarchs to secure political influence against a growing grassroots movement demanding industry accountability. The outcome of these elections will determine whether corporate donors can successfully override public opposition to data centers and emerging tech regulations.

articles.title: The American Worker vs. the Most Qualified
articles.author: polimath
articles.content:
This story started with a rage-bait comment from British tech entrepreneur Paul Graham:
I believe the most qualified person should get the job.
There are many ways to approach this statement, which lives passive-aggressively inside the context of tech hiring and immigration. American tech titan Palmer Luckey grabbed hold of this thread and spent the next few days throttling the life out of it.
Graham took the position that if Luckey hires even one foreign employee, this means that Luckey is betraying his “American firms should hire Americans” stance.
You can read the back-and-forths in voluminous detail. I want to address Graham’s question about “qualified” hiring with a story from my family.
John, the Tool Engineer
John Johnson was drafted into the Army the day before he married Irene. This was inconvenient. A month after his wedding, he took a train from Chicago to Missouri for his basic training.
As part of his Army intake, he filled out many forms. One of them asked if he had any experience with high temperature material work. In between his tool engineering classes at the local community college, John had been working the night shift at a heat treatment company. He marked on his form that he had experience with high-temperatures and, after basic training, he was sent to Huntsville Alabama and assigned to Army Missile Ordinance.
John was to work on developing materials that would survive tremendous heat. Though he was not informed at the time, the goal of this project was to produce materials that would withstand the heat generated during re-entry from space. This was early research into what would become the Apollo heat shield. To test these high-temperature materials, they set a rocket burner horizontally and burned the materials with the rocket blast. John became the military personnel in charge of burner facility 164 HT working alongside German scientist Erich Ball.
It was in this role that John found himself working under Wernher von Braun. His first encounter with Von Braun was when the legendary German scientist wanted to view on of the burner tests to simulate re-entry. von Braun arrived too late and, when he requested to view the test, John (a lowly Specialist 3rd class) followed the safety protocols and denied him entry to the facility viewing bunker. Impressed with John’s bold adherence to the rules, von Braun began calling him “Colonel Johnson” to the annoyance of John’s peers and superiors.
In the ensuing years, John excelled in his role developing re-entry materials. He continued this work as the role evolved from Army Missile Ordinance to the NASA manned space program where he worked as a contractor with Avco. John helped develop heat shields for the Apollo re-entry capsules and the Space Shuttle. When the Apollo 17 launched in 1972, he was the keynote speaker for the Smithsonian Society regarding the mission.
“Most Qualified Person”
The question that Paul Graham is inviting us to ask is “Was John the most qualified person for this job?” The answer is “of course not”. John was 22 years old when he got this job. His had one core qualification (high temperature experience) that put him in this position but there were certainly dozens or even hundreds of more experienced, more qualified engineers from any number of countries who could have taken this position. John didn’t know anything about rockets when he started that job, but he picked it up quickly. He had a core competency, he was eager, he was trainable, and he was diligent. In the course of his work, he impressed the very father of rocket science.
John might not have started as the “most qualified person” but, with a little training and a lot of hard work, he became the most qualified person for the job.
This brings us to Wernher von Braun. If we can take a kid from Chicago, draft him into the Army, and turn him into a lead engineer at NASA, why can’t we develop our own von Braun? Perhaps, given a few decades, we could have. But scientists like von Braun and Erich Ball had irreplicable expertise in the field of rocket science. They didn’t score a few points higher on an aptitude test, they had already built a full rocketry pipeline in Germany and brought with them all the theoretical and practical knowledge that allowed the United States to accelerate our space program.
Importantly, these German scientists were not working in isolation or only among other German scientists and technicians. They were training the next generation of American experts like John. It was never under consideration that we would continuously bring in German factory workers with high temperature experience simply because they had been on the job a year longer than an American worker. The presumption was that the experts we brought in could work alongside American counterparts in order to train up an American workforce to meet the intellectual and engineering demands of manned space flight.
The H-1B program was started with the vision of finding von Brauns across other industries and bringing them into the US. H-1B (supposedly) requires expertise in a specialty occupation in which the applicant has both theoretical and practical application of a body of highly specialized knowledge. This isn’t a description of “the most qualified person”. This is a description of a uniquely qualified person who can offer a leap forward in a specialized field.
Any technical job is going to require some amount of on-the-job training. Every good employee will improve in their role as they become familiar with the organization and the product they are working on. The goal of bringing people in through the H-1B program should include the transmission of expertise and knowledge to the rest of team. An H-1B hire should not simply be marginally better than an American counterpart. They should provide such a leap forward in capabilities such that the rest of the company is elevated in their own knowledge and expertise.
This is why I have so much disdain for Paul Graham accusing Palmer Luckey of duplicity. Graham sees the American economy as something that belongs to the world. He thinks that all businesses (and specifically tech businesses in the United States) are global enterprises that they have no responsibility to train up the next generation of US talent.
Palmer Luckey understands that there is plenty of international talent that can and should be leveraged in the appropriate places and the proper ways. There are many instances where you’re going to want to hire a leading expert in a technical field. But most jobs, the qualifications are a core technical and subject competency combined with diligence and a willingness to learn. There are thousands of young John Johnsons out there who are eager to excel in these jobs. We need to encourage a corporate mindset that believes in the importance of building up the American talent pool to tackle not only the challenge in front of them but the array of challenges that the future will bring.
articles.summary:
Tech entrepreneur Paul Graham and Palmer Luckey are debating the ethics of hiring foreign workers, sparking a broader discussion on the role of H-1B visas in American industry.

### Key Points
- Paul Graham argues that American firms should prioritize hiring domestic talent, while Palmer Luckey defends the strategic use of international expertise.
- The H-1B visa program is intended to bring in uniquely qualified specialists who possess knowledge that can elevate an entire team's capabilities.
- Historical examples, such as the development of Apollo heat shields, demonstrate that foreign experts often serve as mentors to train the next generation of domestic workers.
- Effective hiring strategies should balance immediate technical needs with a long-term commitment to developing a skilled, homegrown workforce.

### Why it Matters
This debate highlights a fundamental tension in the tech sector regarding whether companies have a responsibility to cultivate domestic talent or simply hire the most efficient global labor. By reframing the H-1B program as a tool for knowledge transfer rather than just filling roles, companies can better balance immediate innovation with long-term national workforce development.

articles.title: Why Humans Still Matter in the Age of Intelligent Machines
articles.author: Jonny Caplan
articles.content:
Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
Key Takeaways
- ChatGPT said:
AI shouldn’t replace human creativity, it should amplify it by handling information, research and execution while humans provide instinct and purpose.
- Human experience, irrational confidence and the ability to care deeply about an idea are qualities AI cannot truly replicate.
There is a lot of talk at the moment about what AI is going to replace, and I find the whole conversation slightly backward because we seem obsessed with asking what AI can do that humans currently do, rather than asking what it can never really do and why those differences are actually what could make the relationship between humans and AI so powerful.
For all the extraordinary things AI can do, there are some things it simply cannot replicate in the way a human being experiences them. It can analyze emotion, understand language, recognize patterns and produce something that sounds incredibly sensitive, but it doesn’t actually feel anything. It doesn’t know what it is like to walk into a room and instantly sense that something is wrong before anybody has said a word, or to meet somebody for five minutes and have an inexplicable feeling that you should trust them, or perhaps that you absolutely shouldn’t.
It can understand the language of emotion, but there is a very important difference between understanding an emotion and actually having one.
The same applies to instinct, which I think is one of the most underrated qualities in entrepreneurship. Some of the biggest decisions people make are not based entirely on data, because sometimes you look at something and you simply know that it is right, even though you cannot necessarily explain why.
You cannot always put instinct into a spreadsheet or build a model around it, because instinct is often the accumulated result of everything you have experienced, every mistake you have made, every success you have had, every person you have met and every lesson you have learned, including many of the lessons you didn’t even realize you were learning at the time.
AI doesn’t have that life experience. It has information, an almost absurd amount of information, and it can process that information at a speed and scale that is extraordinary, but it hasn’t actually lived any of it. It hasn’t made a terrible decision at 28 and spent the next ten years remembering exactly why it was terrible.
It hasn’t walked into a meeting completely unprepared and somehow managed to turn it into the best deal of its career.
It hasn’t had somebody tell it that an idea is impossible and then become slightly obsessed with proving them wrong, partly because it believes in the idea and partly because it now really wants to prove that person wrong.
I don’t want AI to be me
All that is exactly why I think AI can be such an extraordinary assistant.
I don’t want it to be me. I want it to be the perfect counterpart to me because the very things that make AI different from us are precisely what make it so useful. I want something sitting there that doesn’t get tired, doesn’t need a coffee, doesn’t have to go home, doesn’t get offended when I say, “No, that’s rubbish, start again,” and doesn’t start wondering whether I have any idea what I am actually doing. I want to be able to throw an idea at it at midnight, completely change my mind twelve minutes later, ask it to approach the whole thing from another direction, decide that direction is terrible, go back to the original idea and then suddenly come up with something completely different, and have it still sitting there ready to help.
It doesn’t moan, it doesn’t sulk, it doesn’t complain that we’ve already done three versions, it doesn’t need a weekend, it doesn’t need a holiday and it doesn’t decide that because somebody else got the better project, it is going to quietly resent me for the next six months. It doesn’t need feeding, it doesn’t need sleeping and, importantly, it doesn’t cheat.
Well, not very often.
AI is occasionally an idiot
It is also, occasionally, an absolute idiot, which I actually find quite reassuring.
You can have a brilliant conversation with AI, get to a genuinely interesting thought, and then suddenly it will confidently tell you something that is completely wrong, misunderstand something you’ve explained three times or produce something that is technically perfect but has absolutely no idea why anybody should care about it. The funny thing is, this makes it considerably more human than some people who are currently predicting the end of humanity, because humans get things spectacularly wrong, too.
The difference is that humans can have a terrible idea and then, five minutes later, have a brilliant one. We can become irrationally passionate about something that nobody else understands, we can take a risk when all the available evidence tells us not to, and we can sometimes be arrogant enough to believe that we can do something everybody else thinks is ridiculous. That arrogance, in the right person and in the right circumstances, can be an incredibly powerful thing because, without a certain amount of irrational confidence, a huge number of businesses, inventions, films, products and ideas would probably never have existed.
And there is some pretty compelling evidence suggesting we are not talking about a distant future here. Stanford’s 2025 AI Index found that 78% of organizations surveyed reported using AI in 2024, up from 55% in 2023, while the proportion using generative AI in at least one business function more than doubled, from 33% to 71%. McKinsey’s research has also found that 64% of respondents say AI is enabling innovation in their organizations, although only 39% report an impact on EBIT at the enterprise level. I think this is an important distinction, because adopting AI and actually knowing how to use it properly are clearly two very different things.
That is the bit I don’t want us to lose.
I don’t want a future where humans start trying to think like machines simply because machines are better at processing information. I want the opposite. I want a future where humans can become even more human because machines take care of more of the things they’re good at.
Steve Jobs put it rather brilliantly when he said, “Technology is nothing. What’s important is that you have a faith in people,” arguing that if you give smart people good tools, they can do wonderful things with them. That was said in 1994, long before anybody was talking about ChatGPT or generative AI, but I actually think it is one of the most relevant observations you can make about where we are heading now, because the technology may be extraordinary, but it is still the person using the technology who decides what is worth creating.
Let’s let humans decide
Let AI do the research. Let it organize the information, find the patterns, challenge the thinking, generate the alternatives, and help turn an idea into something tangible much faster than we could have done before, but let the human decide whether any of it is actually worth doing.
Because creativity isn’t simply the ability to produce ideas. It is the ability to care about an idea enough to pursue it when other people don’t understand it, to recognize something special when it appears in front of you and, perhaps most importantly, to have the courage to back yourself when there isn’t enough evidence yet to prove that you are right.
AI can give you a thousand possibilities, but somebody still has to choose one. It can analyze the market, but somebody still has to walk into the room. It can write the pitch, but somebody still has to stand there and believe in it. It can tell you what the data says, but there will always be moments when an entrepreneur looks at the data and says, “I know what it says, but I don’t believe it.”
And sometimes that person will be completely wrong. But sometimes they will be right, and those are the moments that change everything.
That is why I don’t see AI as the end of human creativity. I see it as potentially the greatest creative partner humans have ever had, because for the first time we can have something sitting alongside us that can absorb an extraordinary amount of information, work at extraordinary speed, never get tired and never get bored, while the human being remains responsible for the things that make the work worth doing in the first place.
The human brings the soul, the instinct, the emotion, the ambition, the experience, the irrational confidence, the humour and, occasionally, the stupidity. AI brings the patience, the memory, the processing power, the research, the speed and the extraordinary willingness to have another go without ever saying, “For God’s sake, we’ve been through this already.”
And maybe that is actually the perfect relationship.
One of us needs sleep, and one of us doesn’t. One of us occasionally has absolutely no idea what we’re doing, and the other one can produce a remarkably convincing answer even when it has absolutely no idea what it is doing either. One of us has instincts, emotions, and a lifetime of experiences that cannot be reduced to data, while the other has access to an enormous amount of knowledge and can help turn those instincts into something real.
That sounds less like a battle between humans and AI to me and much more like the beginning of a very happy marriage.
Provided, of course, the human remembers who is supposed to be in charge.
Key Takeaways
- ChatGPT said:
AI shouldn’t replace human creativity, it should amplify it by handling information, research and execution while humans provide instinct and purpose.
- Human experience, irrational confidence and the ability to care deeply about an idea are qualities AI cannot truly replicate.
There is a lot of talk at the moment about what AI is going to replace, and I find the whole conversation slightly backward because we seem obsessed with asking what AI can do that humans currently do, rather than asking what it can never really do and why those differences are actually what could make the relationship between humans and AI so powerful.
For all the extraordinary things AI can do, there are some things it simply cannot replicate in the way a human being experiences them. It can analyze emotion, understand language, recognize patterns and produce something that sounds incredibly sensitive, but it doesn’t actually feel anything. It doesn’t know what it is like to walk into a room and instantly sense that something is wrong before anybody has said a word, or to meet somebody for five minutes and have an inexplicable feeling that you should trust them, or perhaps that you absolutely shouldn’t.
It can understand the language of emotion, but there is a very important difference between understanding an emotion and actually having one.
articles.summary:
Artificial intelligence should function as a powerful creative partner that amplifies human potential by handling data-heavy tasks while leaving instinct, purpose, and final decision-making to human entrepreneurs.

### Key Points
- Stanford’s 2025 AI Index reports that 78% of organizations used AI in 2024, a significant increase from 55% in 2023.
- McKinsey research indicates that while 64% of organizations use AI for innovation, only 39% report a measurable impact on enterprise-level EBIT.
- AI excels at processing information, recognizing patterns, and maintaining tireless execution, but it lacks genuine human emotion, life experience, and intuition.
- Human qualities like irrational confidence and the ability to care deeply about an idea remain essential for driving business innovation and creative breakthroughs.
- The most effective use of technology involves humans retaining control to determine which ideas are worth pursuing, rather than relying on machines for strategic judgment.

### Why it Matters
The integration of AI into business workflows is rapidly accelerating, yet many organizations struggle to translate these tools into tangible financial results. By positioning AI as a supportive counterpart rather than a replacement, leaders can leverage machine efficiency to enhance the unique, irreplaceable human instincts that drive true innovation.

articles.title: Harvey Smith Explains What Most Games Are Missing And Why He’s Still Making Them: ‘It’s An Act Of Rebellion To Try To Do Something Hopeful In Times Like This’
articles.author: John Walker
articles.content:
Last month, Dishonored co-creator Harvey Smith and Arkane’s former production director Ben Horne announced that they had established a new studio, Black Pony Immersive, with the sole purpose of creating a new immersive sim in the lineage of Deus Ex, Thief, Prey, and System Shock. Insistent on learning more about how the studio came to be and its ambitions for the future, we sat down with Smith and Horne to talk about defying the odds in a precarious gaming industry, the rebellious act of developing in a genre that publishers are afraid to touch, and the deliciousness of mystery. Oh, and what it’s like when you have a limited budget for chairs.
When Arkane Austin was closed by Microsoft in 2024, Harvey Smith and Ben Horne were both beyond devastated. But even among the carnage and sadness, they knew what they were going to do next. Both were of a single mind. In the aftermath of the awful news, Horne came to Smith and said, “You know what we should do?”
“I think I’m going to complete your sentence for you,” Smith replied at the time. “What if we start a studio?”
It wouldn’t be until a year later that Black Pony Immersive was officially formed, and then another year before the studio was unveiled to the public. So what took place in that first year?
“Just talking to every person that we thought might be able to fund us,” says Harvey Smith. “You talk to VCs and they start talking about NFTs or AI, and we’re like, ‘Guys, best of luck.’ You talk to some and they’re like, ‘No, no, we’re not into that at all. We like what you’re about, the fundamentals of your game, but our people are hoping to see, uh, times one thousand return within two years.’”
“You hear a lot of ‘no’s from people,” adds Horne. People asked them, are you guys leveraging any bleeding-edge technology? Or, are we going to get a return on investment super-quickly? “It really sharpened our focus around who are the right partners for us. Not just, ‘how can we get off the ground as quickly as possible?’, which in our hearts is what we wanted to do. We just burned to make this thing, to make this kind of game with these people. But we learned so much about what really matters to us, what we’re willing to accept.”
Eventually, something (and we don’t know what) worked out, leading to Black Pony Immersive receiving enough funding to establish a 26-person studio. “Pretty much no-strings-attached,” adds Smith. “We’re just doing what we think is right every day.”
Of course, this is a far tighter budget than either had been used to after many years as a subsidiary of Bethesda, which is owned by Microsoft. “The downside is you don’t have endless money,” explains Smith. “If you need more money or more people or better chairs, you can’t just snap your fingers and do that. We don’t have any of that, we’re fully remote.” Smith then gestures to the lack of any furniture beneath him. “Uh, I’m standing up.”
“We’re a scrappy little team,” Smith continues, “and we hope to pull off what Looking Glass did, or what Origin did, or what Ion Storm did, or what Arkane and Raphael [Colantonio] certainly did.”
But isn’t there a kind of hubris to this? How many developers have created their own AA team and set out to make the sorts of games they’ve previously achieved under AAA publishers and come up short? “I think my nature…we’re kind of humble,” says Smith in response. “I’ve failed hard a couple of times. Maybe three, depending on how you count it. And it teaches you more than success. Everybody calling you brilliant and loving your shit doesn’t really teach you anything, other than it feels good to be called brilliant.” But then, perhaps there needs to be some boldness too, Smith says. “I don’t want to call it arrogance,” he adds, “but it’s not fair to call it confidence. I’m not the most confident person. It’s some sort of defiance. It’s an act of rebellion to try to do something hopeful in times like this.”
A guiding spirit
There was something unexpectedly poignant about the announcement of Black Pony Immersive. The date of the reveal was planned long in advance, but what no one expected was that the day before, Warren Spector would announce his retirement. Spector, seen by many as the father of the immersive sim genre, has been a close friend and mentor of Harvey Smith’s ever since the latter’s first job as lead tester on System Shock. The pair went on to work together for nine years. The two announcements back to back was, I commented, like a death and a birth.
“I have all these incredible texts back and forth from Warren,” says Smith, immediately emotional. “We’re going to lunch soon to talk about all this, but we did not coordinate this. God, I have such weird feelings about this, because on one hand, well deserved! And watching the whole industry go through turmoil is so hard on the soul, right? Trying to go to bat over and over and having a tidal wave hit you is very difficult. But, at the same time, it’s sad too, because you want to see people keep doing what they do well forever. He’s amazing.”
“And the guy’s 70,” I interject. “True,” says Smith. “I never could have asked for a more patient, exuberant mentor. And I learned so much. I’m eternally thankful to Warren.”
When the Heart speaks
One of Harvey Smith’s driving passions is to create games that stay with players long after they’ve finished them, games that “get into their fucking heads, and they talk about for 10, 20 years, and you can see the delight, the cartharis. I have so many letters, I save all those…we had a fucking wedding.”
A wedding?
“For Dishonored. These two amazing people wanted to get married, someone reached out and said they want to theme it all Dishonored, it’s all going to be in costumes.”
The PR team in London told Smith about this and asked if he’d write a few lines for the Heart. Something for the couple to have read out at their wedding. The Heart was one of the most fascinating parts of Dishonored, a literal heart, once belonging to Jessamine Kaldwin, that you could hold and that would offer poetic insights into the NPCs in the game’s world, a wholly optional feature that gave the setting of Dunwall so much more color.
Smith continues, “I sat down and immediately wrote a bunch of lines from the perspective of the Heart. I texted April Stewart who did the voice for Jessamine and the Heart [and also plays Cartman’s mom on South Park] and I explained what was happening. She was like, ‘Oh my God, I’m gonna go to the kitchen right now, my partner and I are going to record these lines on my iPhone.’”
It didn’t stop there. “I went to Thomas Mitton and said, ‘Hey dude, we’ve gotta do some more Heart lines.’ He’s like, ‘But we’re not working on a project!’ [I said] ‘I know, I know, but check it out!’”
Mitton was also immediately on board. “So all the reverb and wind sounds and the heart beating and the echoing voice and all that shit, he recorded them, and so we sent them to the PR team, and they were like, ‘What the fuck?!’”
At the wedding, one member of the couple held up a Dishonored Heart that someone had made, and they played the lines over the speakers. The lines were written from the perspective of one person analyzing the other person to see if they were the right match.”
All the way through this anecdote, Ben Horne was audibly gasping, sitting more and more upright in his chair as the tale went on. Even he’d never heard about this before. Smith explains, “There’s more lucrative stuff to do, there’s saner stuff, and there’s stuff that hurts less when it goes bad. But the reason you do it—cynical people call it parasocial, but it’s this connection with the audience, and if you’re a musician or a writer or a filmmaker, a video game maker—if you know you know. It’s very powerful because you’re not doing this shit for yourself. Nobody’s writing a novel and then pitching it into the fucking fireplace. It’s so hard to write a book, and it’s so hard to make a game. So you’re doing it for this connection between humans.”
Embracing the mystery
Black Pony Immersive is not ready to talk about the game it’s working on, but I wanted to get an idea of why it’s working on one. What is the ambition behind the project?
“You know, the longer you’re in games,” Smith muses, “the more you see the same model play out over and over. And then somebody suddenly does something that feels fresh. Like [2021’s creepy deckbuilder] Inscryption, it had a sense of mystery in it, and I so rarely see mystery in games. Real mystery. Games are about systems and UI and pointers to the player, and helping the player understand what’s happening in this weird tech that you’re interacting with, right? So technology works against mystery. And Inscryption came out, and it had this feeling of mystery that I loved so much; it was delicious.”
Around the same time, Smith points out, Elden Ring also came out. “I had bounced off all the Souls games, but in Elden Ring you just wander around Limgrave and you hear that music, and you’re just constantly possessed with ‘what is around the corner?’” He tails off for a moment, and then reminds himself he can’t get into any specifics. “Doing something that is magical like that, that even if you’ve played games for 30, 40, 50 years, it feels novel in some way, it feels special, it feels like someone loved this and gave it their all, it feels like it has a voice, people still talk about it in 10 years. That would make me feel successful.”
Smith remembers sitting next to the FTL designers at an awards show, and wanting to spend the entire evening telling them not just why he loved their game, but stories from it, anecdotes about specific adventures.
He then recalls a line from Doug Church, the project lead on System Shock, who said, “When a game really works, people get together later and tell stories as if it actually happened. As if they played football, or went to war, together.”
Smith says this is what he wants from his game. “That joy, that magic between people.”
articles.summary:
Dishonored co-creator Harvey Smith and former Arkane director Ben Horne have launched Black Pony Immersive, a new independent studio dedicated to developing original immersive simulation video games.

### Key Points
- Black Pony Immersive is a 26-person, fully remote studio founded by Harvey Smith and Ben Horne following the 2024 closure of Arkane Austin.
- The founders secured independent, no-strings-attached funding after rejecting venture capital offers that prioritized rapid returns or specific technology trends like AI and NFTs.
- The studio aims to create immersive sims in the tradition of genre-defining titles such as *Deus Ex*, *Thief*, *Prey*, and *System Shock*.
- Smith and Horne are prioritizing creative freedom and long-term player connection over the high-budget, high-pressure constraints of AAA publishing.
- The studio’s development philosophy focuses on fostering mystery and player-driven storytelling, drawing inspiration from titles like *Inscryption* and *Elden Ring*.

### Why it Matters
The formation of Black Pony Immersive represents a significant pushback against the industry trend of consolidating talent into massive, risk-averse AAA studios. By operating as a small, independent team, the founders are attempting to preserve the niche immersive sim genre while proving that creative, player-focused experiences can thrive outside of traditional corporate structures.

articles.title: Dropbox breach seemingly caused by egregious authentication failure [U]
articles.author: Ben Lovejoy
articles.content:
Multiple Dropbox users have been emailed by the cloud storage company to advise them that a security breach saw unauthorised access to their account. Update: the company has said that about 5,000 accounts were compromised, with files downloaded from around 1,500 of them.
The root cause appears to be a lack of authentication by Dropbox when attackers created a single sign-on option through a third-party company …
Developer Yoni Levy posted a copy of the email he received on X.
We are writing to let you know that we’ve observed unauthorized access to your Dropbox account between August 4 and August 21, 2026. While our logs show no evidence that your files were viewed or downloaded, we want to share with you what happened, what we are doing about it, and what additional steps you can take.
Other Dropbox users reported receiving the same email in which the company said it resulted from a problem with a single sign-on (SSO) option using Lenovo IDs.
Dropbox partners with Lenovo as an identity provider so that users can log in to their Dropbox accounts using verified Lenovo IDs. While you may not have an existing Lenovo ID, our investigation determined that an issue with Lenovo’s email verification process allowed an unauthorized party to register a Lenovo ID using your email address and then use that Lenovo ID to log into the Dropbox account associated with that email address.
However, while Dropbox claims the flaw was in Lenovo’s email verification process, the bigger issue appears to be that Dropbox itself did not require users to use their existing login to verify the new SSO, as The CyberSec Guru reports.
- Recon/selection: The attacker compiles target email addresses (breach corpora, LinkedIn, customer lists — email addresses are effectively public data).
- Rogue IdP enrollment: The attacker registers a Lenovo ID as victim@example.com . No inbox access is needed because Lenovo’s verification step is missing or bypassable. The display name is set to something disposable — one victim who reclaimed the rogue account found the name “John Madden,” the late NFL broadcaster, a strong tell of bulk, low-effort registration.
- Federated sign-in: The attacker clicks “Continue with Lenovo” on Dropbox. Lenovo’s authorization server issues a token whose email claim matches the victim’s Dropbox account.
- Implicit account linking: Dropbox resolves the email claim to the existing account and mints a session. No password prompt, no step-up, no “link this new identity?” consent. From Dropbox’s perspective, a trusted IdP had already vouched for the address.
9to5Mac’s Take
While there was certainly a failure to verify email addresses at the Lenovo end, it would not have done any harm if Dropbox had authenticated the linked ID before it could be used to sign in. Failing to do so is an egregious fault.
The company has now fixed the flaw and expired all sessions previously ‘authenticated’ through a Lenovo ID.
If you don’t already have two-factor authentication enabled for Dropbox, it is highly recommended to change this immediately.
Photo by Shubham Dhage on Unsplash
articles.summary:
Dropbox has confirmed a security breach affecting approximately 5,000 user accounts, caused by a flaw in the single sign-on integration process between the cloud provider and Lenovo.

### Key Points
- Unauthorized access occurred between August 4 and August 21, 2026, with files downloaded from roughly 1,500 accounts.
- The vulnerability stemmed from a Lenovo email verification process that allowed attackers to register accounts using victims' email addresses.
- Dropbox failed to require secondary authentication or user consent when linking new Lenovo IDs to existing Dropbox accounts.
- The company has since patched the security flaw and terminated all active sessions authenticated through the compromised Lenovo ID integration.
- Users are strongly encouraged to enable two-factor authentication to protect their accounts from future unauthorized access attempts.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the significant security risks associated with federated identity systems when platforms fail to implement rigorous account-linking protocols. It serves as a critical reminder for users to maintain multi-factor authentication, as even trusted third-party integrations can become vectors for unauthorized data access.

articles.title: CartographAI Launched To Help Advertisers Pick The Right Tech Vendors. Now, It’s Helping Vendors Market Themselves, Too
articles.author: Anthony Vargas
articles.content:
With so many ad tech vendors to choose from, where should brands and agencies begin?
CartographAI, a new startup from two buy-side veterans, wants to help advertisers pick the right tech partners by using assessment criteria that weigh what media buyers actually care about, rather than publicly-available marketing materials.
CartographAI is the brainchild of former Goodway Group CEO Jay Friedman and Danilo Tauro, a former McKinsey analyst who also previously headed up Procter & Gamble’s vendor analysis and risk assessments. They told AdExchanger they launched the endeavor earlier this year to disrupt the industry’s traditional consultancies that advise advertisers on tech strategy as well as the analyst model that anoints certain companies as leaders in their categories.
Instead of compiling a one-size-fits-all list of what it believes are the top tech vendors in the industry like other analysts, Friedman said, CartographAI helps individual brands and agencies find the right fit for them, which might not always be the industry-consensus category leaders.
In addition to helping buyers compare different competitive solutions, a big part of the company’s value prop is simply breaking down what various tech vendors do in a more straightforward way than you can find on their websites. According to Tauro, some agencies who have tested the solution said, “It’s like the Lumascape, but you can double-click the logos.”
CartographAI’s vendor-ranking solution started as a brand- and agency-focused product, and those groups will remain its core constituencies, Friedman and Tauro said.
But the company is also launching an accelerator program to help tech vendors more effectively market their solutions to advertisers, it announced this week.
Marketing to marketers
The accelerator program has already assembled a roster of ad tech vendors, including The Trade Desk, Viant, MNTN, Adelaide, Optable, Chalice, Gamera, Clinch, Evertune, Eulerity, TAU, Bright Mountain, Version2, NativeAds, QRate and Narrative.
For between $1,000 and $3,000 a month, depending on the company’s size and growth stage, Friedman said, vendors can sign up to get “deep, analyst-level intel on your subcategory” on a monthly call with CartographAI and its team of subject-matter experts. These experts are drawn from Friedman’s and Tauro’s industry contacts, including from the Procter & Gamble digital alumni forum.
The experts give vendors insight, sourced from direct conversations with buyers, into what advertisers are looking for in their tech solutions, Tauro said. These insights can inform not only the vendors’ product road maps but how they market their solutions.
Plus, CartographAI will promote accelerator program participants on social media and in podcasts and newsletters, and vendors also get access to co-marketing opportunities with CartographAI at ad industry events.
The accelerator program is particularly valuable for helping an ad tech startup like Gamera, a media quality platform that launched in 2022, get its product in front of the right people, said its CEO and co-founder, Gareth Glaser. “It helps us identify the right contacts at brands, agencies, trading desks and everything in between without going through a long series of false starts, while also providing an objective, concise way to communicate what our product does and why it matters.”
Having that clear path into the buy-side market is one thing, Glaser said, but it also comes “with guidance from people who understand how to create the right conversations and, just as importantly, avoid the unproductive ones.”
Attention measurement platform Adelaide is early in its journey with CartographAI’s accelerator program, Adelaide CEO Marc Guldimann said, but the company already received plenty of valuable feedback on its go-to-market strategy during the onboarding process.
“Jay has a [Charlie-]Munger-like command of incentives in the ecosystem and Danilo is super strategic,” Guldimann said. “Advice and blunt feedback from a team with this kind of understanding of the market is invaluable.”
In addition, later this year, CartographAI plans to launch an AI analyst solution grounded on its industry expertise that will advise advertisers on which vendors can help them solve particular challenges or drive certain KPIs.
Given that planned rollout, Glaser said, “CartographAI is laying important groundwork for a future in which buyers increasingly use AI to discover, evaluate and engage with new technology partners.”
Ranking the vendors
Until the AI analyst launches, advertisers can access CartographAI’s vendor rankings through its website, which is live with about 1,000 rankings today and about 20 new company profiles added per month. The website rankings are free to access; clients just have to sign up for a login.
CartographAI groups ad tech vendors into different vertical market categories. For example, it has a category for DSPs and another for identity resolution/ID graph providers/DMPs.
It then ranks the vendors according to five criteria that are unique to their vertical market, labeling their offerings as either “emerging,” “capable” or “advanced” in each of those five criteria. For instance, the identity solution category’s criteria include match quality, coverage and portability, privacy and consent mechanics, activation utility and commercial and dependency risk.
On top of using the free site rankings, brands and agencies can also sign up for a more traditional white glove consulting service. Each of these deals is priced on a custom basis, with CartographAI charging between five and six figures for consulting, Friedman said, although it’s still solidifying the economics of this offering.
Once the company’s AI analyst is ready for market, it should help further streamline how brands and agencies run their RFPs when onboarding new vendors, Tauro said.
In his experience, he said, buyers can spend six-plus months evaluating new partners, with about two months spent simply learning everything they can about the particular product category. That’s why CartographAI prioritizes connecting advertisers with experts who are already knowledgeable about the different vertical ad tech markets – and why it’s training its AI on their expertise.
“It’s almost a marketplace of knowledge,” Tauro said. “The point is helping that translation between how marketers think, talk and operate, and how tech companies do.”

Startup CartographAI, founded by industry veterans Jay Friedman and Danilo Tauro, provides advertisers with objective vendor assessments and an accelerator program to streamline ad tech procurement processes.

### Key Points
- CartographAI offers free, criteria-based rankings for approximately 1,000 ad tech vendors, categorizing them as emerging, capable, or advanced.
- The company launched an accelerator program for vendors like The Trade Desk and Adelaide, charging $1,000 to $3,000 monthly for market insights and co-marketing.
- Founders Jay Friedman and Danilo Tauro utilize their backgrounds from Goodway Group and Procter & Gamble to provide expert-led, buy-side focused consulting services.
- A proprietary AI analyst tool is scheduled for release later this year to help brands automate vendor discovery and RFP evaluations.
- The platform aims to reduce the typical six-month vendor evaluation cycle by translating complex technical offerings into actionable, buyer-centric language.

### Why it Matters
This platform addresses the fragmentation of the ad tech market by providing a transparent, data-driven alternative to traditional industry analyst reports. By aligning vendor capabilities with specific advertiser needs, CartographAI helps brands reduce procurement friction and make more informed technology investments.

articles.title: U.S. Futures Steady as Investors Monitor Oil Prices, Fed Data and Bond Yields: Dow Jones, S&P, Nasdaq, Wall Street
articles.author: Fiona Craig
articles.content:

U.S. stock futures were little changed on Wednesday as investors awaited U.S. economic data and the Federal Reserve’s Beige Book while monitoring developments involving the United States and Iran and further increases in global government bond yields.
S&P 500 Futures were flat at 7,637.5 points as of 03:20 ET, while Nasdaq 100 Futures were unchanged at 29,112 points. Dow Jones Futures gained 0.17% to 52,914 points.
The moves followed a lower session on Wall Street, where major indexes declined by as much as 1% at the start of September.
Investors continued to monitor the Middle East after the United States carried out another round of strikes against Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, representing the second U.S. attack on Iran during the week.
The status of the Strait of Hormuz remains disputed. The United States says the waterway remains open to commercial shipping, while Iran says it remains closed.
Developments in the region have contributed to higher oil prices, increasing market attention on the potential implications for inflation and monetary policy.
Investors are also awaiting U.S. economic data and the Federal Reserve’s Beige Book for additional information on economic activity, employment and inflation.
Markets are assessing whether inflation remains elevated enough to keep interest rates higher or whether signs of slower economic and labour-market activity could eventually provide central banks with scope to adjust monetary policy.
The Bank of Canada’s policy communication is also being monitored as investors assess how central banks are responding to inflation, economic growth and elevated borrowing costs.
Any implications for future monetary policy remain dependent on incoming economic data and central-bank decisions.
Government bond yields continued to move higher across several major markets.
The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield was approaching 5%, near a three-year high. Australia’s 10-year government bond yield reached its highest level in more than 15 years, while Japan’s 10-year yield was trading around levels not seen for approximately three decades.
Higher government bond yields can affect equities by increasing the returns available from fixed-income securities relative to stocks and by raising financing costs across the economy.
They can also increase the discount rates used to value future corporate cash flows, which can have a greater effect on companies whose valuations depend heavily on earnings expected further into the future, including some growth and technology stocks.
Investors are therefore monitoring several factors simultaneously, including elevated bond yields, higher oil prices, developments involving the United States and Iran, and the outlook for Federal Reserve policy.
The direction of monetary policy will depend on subsequent inflation, economic and labour-market data, as well as decisions and communications from policymakers.

- The Bank of Canada’s recent policy communications are under scrutiny as global central banks navigate the balance between economic growth and elevated borrowing costs.
